10.1016/j.beproc.2004.08.007.citation: Higa, J. J., & Simm, L. A. (2004). Interval timing in Siamese fighting fish (Betta splendens). Behavioural Processes, 67, 501-509. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.beproc.2004.08.007
10.1016/j.beproc.2004.08.007.figure: Fig. 2 (cumulative records per subject and condition)
10.1016/j.beproc.2004.08.007.expected: Few responses early in each interval; the response rate rises as the interval elapses, either gradually (a scallop) or after a break point.
10.1016/j.beproc.2004.08.007.notes: The paper's reinforcer is 20 s of a reflective mirror, and each interval is timed from the end of the previous reinforcer. contingency-py times FI from reinforcer onset, so a 20-s reinforcer would leave a 10-s interval after it; the reinforcer is shortened to 0.5 s so that the interval after each reinforcer stays close to 30 s.

10.1901/jeab.2005.71-04.citation: Leslie, J. C., Shaw, D., Gregg, G., McCormick, N., Reynolds, D. S., & Dawson, G. R. (2005). Effects of reinforcement schedule on facilitation of operant extinction by chlordiazepoxide. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 84, 327-338. https://doi.org/10.1901/jeab.2005.71-04
10.1901/jeab.2005.71-04.figure: Fig. 1, lower panel (cumulative record of responses 31-60 in the last training session)
10.1901/jeab.2005.71-04.expected: After each lever presentation a pause of variable length, then fast responding until the reinforcer (break-and-run).
10.1901/jeab.2005.71-04.notes: The paper runs discrete trials: lever insertion, FR 5, then a pellet, lever withdrawal and a 1-min intertrial interval. The DSL has no intertrial interval, so a 60-s reinforcer stands in for it; the subject's time since reinforcement restarts at reinforcer onset, so its pause is measured from the end of the 60 s.

10.1007/bf03394799.citation: Weiner, H. (1982). Histories of response omission and human operant behavior under a fixed-ratio schedule of reinforcement. The Psychological Record, 32, 409-434. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03394799
10.1007/bf03394799.figure: Fig. 2 (cumulative records of the first and eighth sessions)
10.1007/bf03394799.expected: Constant responding without post-reinforcement pauses: an almost straight cumulative record.
10.1007/bf03394799.notes: The paper's sessions last 30 min; 100 reinforcers at 3 responses/s take about 23 min. The rise in rate from the first to the eighth session is not compared: a Poisson subject does not change across sessions.

10.1901/jeab.1968.11-s327.citation: Catania, A. C., & Reynolds, G. S. (1968). A quantitative analysis of the responding maintained by interval schedules of reinforcement. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 11, 327-383. https://doi.org/10.1901/jeab.1968.11-s327
10.1901/jeab.1968.11-s327.figure: Fig. 13 (constant-probability VI, one whole session); Fig. 4 (arithmetic VI 108-s) is not comparable
10.1901/jeab.1968.11-s327.expected: A roughly constant rate within each interval, without marked pauses or acceleration after reinforcement.
10.1901/jeab.1968.11-s327.notes: The extracted DSL has no @algorithm; one is added so the Fleshler-Hoffman sequence is reproducible. contingency-py's VI is constant-probability (Fleshler-Hoffman) only, so the run is compared with the paper's constant-probability figure (Fig. 13), not with the arithmetic VI 108-s of Fig. 4, whose upward-concave intervals this engine cannot produce. The mean interval stays 108 s.

10.1901/jeab.1969.12-887.citation: Stubbs, D. A., & Pliskoff, S. S. (1969). Concurrent responding with fixed relative rate of reinforcement. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 12, 887-895. https://doi.org/10.1901/jeab.1969.12-887
10.1901/jeab.1969.12-887.figure: Fig. 1 (relative response rate, relative time and relative local rate against relative reinforcement rate; COD 2 s)
10.1901/jeab.1969.12-887.expected: Relative response rate on key A close to the relative reinforcement rate (about 0.75 in the VI 1-min / VI 3-min condition).
10.1901/jeab.1969.12-887.notes: The paper uses a Findley procedure (one main key and a changeover key, COD 2 s). The extracted DSL is a two-key Conc without COD; the run adds COD=2s and keeps two keys. contingency-py holds a reinforcer set up during the COD. The subject is trained for five sessions with the same DSL (same Fleshler-Hoffman sequence) and only the last session is judged.
